title: Angels in Worship, Law and Story
bigQuestion: What jobs do angels do in the Bible's stories, and why do the texts insist that they are never to be worshiped?

story.title: Get Up, I Am a Servant Too
story.kicker: Near the end of Revelation, John falls at an angel's feet, and the angel tells him to stop.
paragraphs: The book of Revelation says it was written by a man named John on the island of Patmos, off the coast of what is now Turkey (Revelation 1:9). It is full of visions. John sees thrones, lampstands, sealed scrolls and a city of gold. Angels guide him through much of it. They show him scenes and explain what they mean.

In Revelation 19, an angel tells John to write down a blessing on those invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb. John is overwhelmed. He falls at the angel's feet to worship him. The angel stops him at once: "See thou do it not: I am thy fellowservant, and of thy brethren that have the testimony of Jesus: worship God."

Then, near the very end of the book, it happens again. In Revelation 22:8 to 9, John says that when he had heard and seen these things, he fell down to worship before the feet of the angel who showed them to him. The angel gives almost the same answer. He is a fellow servant with John, with the prophets and with all who keep the words of the book. Worship God.

Readers have long noticed that the scene appears twice. Some think the repetition is there on purpose, to make the lesson impossible to miss. The angel does not scold John or frighten him. He simply puts himself on the same level as John, as a servant, and points away from himself.

Michael Heiser treated scenes like this as an important key to how the Bible talks about angels. They are powerful and they serve, but worship is for God alone. In this chapter you will follow angels through the giving of the law, the worship of heaven, the Gospel stories and later Jewish writings, and see how that key keeps turning up.
story.think: The angel calls himself John's fellow servant. What does that phrase say about how the angel sees himself compared to John?

lessons.title: A Fiery Law and Holy Ones
lessons.mainIdea: Deuteronomy 33:2 links Sinai with God's holy ones, and the Greek Septuagint names angels there directly.
reading: Exodus 19 and 20 tell of God giving the law at Mount *Sinai* with thunder, fire and a thick cloud. Those chapters do not mention angels. But a later poem does. In Deuteronomy 33:2, Moses blesses the tribes and says that the LORD came from Sinai. In the King James Version, he came "with ten thousands of saints," and from his right hand went "a fiery law." The Hebrew for saints here is qedoshim, holy ones.

The Hebrew of this verse is hard. The words translated "fiery law" are unusual, and scholars still debate them. The *Septuagint*, the ancient Greek translation made in the centuries before Jesus, reads the end of the verse differently. It says that at God's right hand there were angels with him. So in the Greek, the angels at Sinai are named outright. A difference like this between two forms of a text is called a *variant*.

Psalm 68:17 adds another picture. It says the chariots of God are twenty thousand, and the Lord is among them, as in Sinai. Heiser read these verses together. In his view, the Hebrew Bible pictures God at Sinai surrounded by his heavenly host, and the Septuagint made that picture plainer. Other scholars read the Hebrew holy ones as possibly Israel's own people, or stress how uncertain the verse is.

words.d: the mountain where, in Exodus, God gives Israel the law
the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, begun in the 200s BCE
a difference in wording between two copies or versions of the same text

look.title: The LORD Came From Sinai
look.text: The LORD came from Sinai, and rose up from Seir unto them; he shined forth from mount Paran, and he came with ten thousands of saints: from his right hand went a fiery law for them.
look.prompt: The Greek Septuagint ends this verse with angels at God's right hand. Which words in the English here might a reader connect with angels, and why?

check.q: Which version of Deuteronomy 33:2 names angels with God directly?
check.why: The Septuagint says angels were at God's right hand. The Hebrew speaks of holy ones and a hard phrase often read as fiery law.

check.q: What does the Hebrew word behind "saints" in Deuteronomy 33:2 mean?
check.why: The Hebrew is qedoshim, holy ones, the same word used for God's heavenly assembly in Psalm 89.

check.q: What is a variant?
choices: A difference in wording between versions of a text
A song sung in the temple
check.why: A variant is a place where two copies or versions of a text read differently, like the Hebrew and Greek of Deuteronomy 33:2.

lessons.title: The Law Given Through Angels
lessons.mainIdea: Three New Testament passages say the law came through angels, a tradition shared with other Jewish writings of the time.
reading: In Acts 7, Stephen speaks before the council in Jerusalem. He ends by saying his hearers "received the law by the disposition of angels, and have not kept it" (7:53). Paul writes in Galatians 3:19 that the law "was ordained by angels in the hand of a *mediator*." Hebrews 2:2 calls the law "the word spoken by angels." Three different writers assume the same thing. Angels had a part in giving the law at Sinai.

This idea was not new with the New Testament. The book of *Jubilees*, written in Hebrew around the 100s BCE, retells Genesis and part of Exodus. In it, an angel of the presence writes out history for Moses on the mountain (Jubilees 1:27 to 2:1). Jubilees is part of the Bible only in the Ethiopian Orthodox Church. Its wide use shows how Jewish readers of the time imagined Sinai.

Heiser argued that the New Testament writers drew on this shared *tradition*, which grew from verses like Deuteronomy 33:2. Readers differ on why each writer mentions it. In Galatians, many scholars think Paul uses it to say the law came less directly than God's promise to Abraham. In Hebrews, the point is that if the word spoken by angels was binding, the message spoken by the Son matters even more.

words.d: a go-between who carries terms or words between two parties
a Jewish retelling of Genesis and Exodus from about the 100s BCE; canonical in the Ethiopian Orthodox Church
beliefs and stories handed down within a community over time

look.title: Three Writers, One Tradition
look.text: Acts 7:53: you received the law by the disposition of angels. Galatians 3:19: the law was ordained by angels in the hand of a mediator. Hebrews 2:2: the word spoken by angels was steadfast.
look.prompt: Each writer mentions angels and the law for a different purpose. Pick one verse, read the verses around it, and explain what point the writer is making.

check.q: Who says in Acts 7:53 that the law was received by the disposition of angels?
check.why: Stephen says this at the end of his speech before the council in Acts 7.

check.q: In Jubilees, who writes out history for Moses on the mountain?
check.why: Jubilees 1:27 to 2:1 has an angel of the presence write for Moses at Sinai.

check.q: What point do many scholars think Paul makes in Galatians 3:19?
choices: That the law came less directly than God's promise to Abraham
That the law was never given
check.why: Paul contrasts the law, given through angels and a mediator, with the promise God spoke directly to Abraham.

lessons.title: "See Thou Do It Not"
lessons.mainIdea: In Revelation, an angel twice refuses John's worship and calls himself a fellow servant.
reading: In Revelation 19:10 and again in 22:8 to 9, John falls down before an angel to *worship* him. Both times the angel stops him. He says he is John's *fellowservant*. He is a servant like John, the prophets and all who keep the words of the book. Both times he ends with two words: worship God.

The angel's answer rests on an old command. Exodus 20:3 says, "Thou shalt have no other gods before me." The Shema in Deuteronomy 6:4 calls Israel to love the LORD alone. The angel is glorious and has just shown John great visions. Even so, the text puts him on John's side of the line, among those who serve, and not among those who receive worship.

Heiser pointed to these scenes to show that the heavenly host serves God and does not share his place. He argued that the Bible can call heavenly beings elohim and still hold that only one elohim, the God of Israel, is to be worshiped. Jewish and Christian readers of every kind have read these scenes as a clear warning against giving worship to angels.

words.d: honor and devotion given to God, often shown by bowing or kneeling
one who serves the same master; the angel's word for himself in Revelation 19 and 22
Deuteronomy 6:4-9, a central Jewish declaration that the LORD is one

look.title: Worship God
look.text: And when I had heard and seen, I fell down to worship before the feet of the angel which shewed me these things. Then saith he unto me, See thou do it not: for I am thy fellowservant, and of thy brethren the prophets, and of them which keep the sayings of this book: worship God.
look.prompt: List the three groups the angel says he belongs with. What do those groups have in common?

check.q: What does the angel call himself when he stops John?
check.why: In Revelation 19:10 and 22:9 the angel says, "I am thy fellowservant."

check.q: How many times in Revelation does John fall down to worship an angel?
check.why: It happens in Revelation 19:10 and again in Revelation 22:8-9.

check.q: Which older command does the angel's answer rest on?
choices: Thou shalt have no other gods before me
Honor thy father and thy mother
check.why: Exodus 20:3 forbids having other gods. The angel points John to worship God alone.

lessons.title: Colossians 2:18: Two Readings
lessons.mainIdea: Colossians 2:18 warns about the worship of angels, and scholars read the phrase in two main ways.
reading: Paul's letter to the Colossians warns its readers about teachers who were judging them. In the King James Version, Colossians 2:18 says, "Let no man beguile you of your reward in a voluntary humility and worshipping of angels, intruding into those things which he hath not seen." The key phrase in Greek is thrēskeia tōn angelōn, "worship of the angels."

The phrase is *ambiguous*, meaning it can be read more than one way. In the first reading, it means worship given to angels. Some people in Colossae, on this view, were honoring angels in a way the letter rejects. In the second reading, it means the worship that angels offer. On this view, some teachers claimed to join the angels' worship in heaven through visions, and looked down on those who did not.

Both readings have strong defenders. The second reading gained support after the Dead Sea Scrolls showed Jewish groups who hoped to join the worship of angels. Either way, the letter's answer is the same. Colossians 2:19 says the readers should hold fast to the head, which in this letter is Christ. Heiser read the New Testament as keeping angels in a supporting role, serving God and never sharing his worship.

words.d: able to be read in more than one way
an ancient town in what is now western Turkey, home of the church Colossians addresses
a scene seen in a dream or trance, often reported as coming from God

look.title: Worship of the Angels
look.text: Reading 1: the Colossians were being urged to give worship to angels. Reading 2: some teachers claimed, through visions, to join in the worship the angels offer in heaven. The Greek phrase is the same in both: worship of the angels.
look.prompt: Which words in Colossians 2:18, such as "intruding into those things which he hath not seen," might support each reading? Explain one.

check.q: In the second reading of Colossians 2:18, what does "worship of angels" mean?
choices: Worship that people give to angels
The worship that angels themselves offer in heaven
check.why: The second reading takes the phrase as the angels' own worship, which some teachers claimed to join through visions.

check.q: What discovery gave support to the second reading?
check.why: The Dead Sea Scrolls show Jewish groups who hoped to join the worship of angels, which made the second reading more likely to some scholars.

check.q: What does ambiguous mean?
choices: Able to be read in more than one way
check.why: An ambiguous phrase can fairly be read more than one way, like worship of the angels in Colossians 2:18.

lessons.title: Songs of the Sabbath Sacrifice
lessons.mainIdea: A Dead Sea Scrolls text pictures angels as priests leading worship in a heavenly temple.
reading: In caves near Qumran, by the Dead Sea, scholars found copies of a work now called the *Songs of the Sabbath Sacrifice*. More copies turned up at Masada, the desert fortress. The work has thirteen songs, one for each of the first thirteen Sabbaths of the year. The copies date from about the first century BCE to the first century CE.

The songs do not describe worship on earth. They call on heavenly beings to praise God in a heavenly *sanctuary*. The songs call these beings elohim, holy ones and chief princes. They describe them as priests who serve before God. Later songs picture the heavenly temple itself, its chariot-throne and its cherubim, joining in praise. The people who sang these songs seem to have hoped their worship on earth matched the worship above.

The Songs help readers see the Jewish world around the New Testament. They show how Isaiah 6 and Ezekiel 1 were read and expanded. Heiser's 2004 dissertation studied the divine council in Second Temple Jewish writings, the period of texts like these. The Songs also show why some scholars read Colossians 2:18 as being about joining the angels' worship. The singers praise God alongside the angels. They do not worship the angels themselves.

words.d: a Dead Sea Scrolls work of thirteen songs describing angels' worship in heaven
the site by the Dead Sea near the caves where most of the Dead Sea Scrolls were found
a holy place for worship; here, the heavenly temple

look.title: Where the Copies Were Found
look.cite: Songs of the Sabbath Sacrifice: 4Q400-407, 11Q17, and the Masada copy; standard scholarly counts
look.prompt: What does finding ten copies in two places suggest about how the Songs were used?

check.q: How many songs are in the Songs of the Sabbath Sacrifice?
check.why: The work has thirteen songs, one for each of the first thirteen Sabbaths of the year.

check.q: How do the Songs describe the angels?
choices: As priests who serve in a heavenly sanctuary
check.why: The Songs call the heavenly beings elohim and chief princes and describe them as priests serving before God.

check.q: Besides Qumran, where were copies of the Songs found?
check.why: A copy of the Songs was also found at Masada, the desert fortress by the Dead Sea.

lessons.title: Messengers at the Births
lessons.mainIdea: In Matthew and Luke, angels bring news of the births of John and Jesus, often starting with "Fear not."
reading: Luke's Gospel opens in the Jerusalem temple. An angel appears to an old priest named Zechariah beside the altar of incense. He says he is *Gabriel*, who stands in the presence of God (Luke 1:19). He announces that Zechariah's wife Elizabeth will have a son, John. Six months later, Gabriel goes to Nazareth and tells a young woman named Mary that she will bear a son, Jesus (Luke 1:26 to 38). This scene is called the *Annunciation*.

Then, outside Bethlehem, an angel of the Lord appears to shepherds at night. He tells them a Savior is born. Suddenly a multitude of the heavenly host appears, praising God (Luke 2:8 to 14). Matthew tells the story from Joseph's side. An angel of the Lord speaks to Joseph three times in dreams, in Matthew 1:20, 2:13 and 2:19. The angel tells him to take Mary as his wife, to flee to Egypt, and to return.

The angels in these stories are messengers in the plain sense of mal'ak and angelos. They bring news and instructions. Again and again they begin with "Fear not." In the Bible, meeting a being from God's presence is overwhelming, and these words calm the hearer. Readers of every tradition have loved these scenes. Christmas music and art have retold them for centuries.

words.d: the angel who announces the births of John and Jesus in Luke 1
the scene in Luke 1:26-38 where Gabriel tells Mary she will bear Jesus
the great company of angels who praise God before the shepherds in Luke 2:13

look.title: Angels in the Birth Stories
look.prompt: Who does the angel speak to in Matthew, and who in Luke? What might that tell you about each writer's focus?

check.q: In Luke 1, to whom does Gabriel first appear?
check.why: Gabriel appears first to the priest Zechariah in the temple, then six months later to Mary.

check.q: In Matthew, how does the angel of the Lord speak to Joseph?
check.why: Matthew 1:20, 2:13 and 2:19 all describe an angel speaking to Joseph in a dream.

check.q: What words do the birth-story angels often begin with?
check.why: The angels say "Fear not" to Zechariah, Mary, the shepherds and Joseph, to calm people who are overwhelmed.

lessons.title: Angels at the Empty Tomb
lessons.mainIdea: All four Gospels place heavenly messengers at Jesus' empty tomb, though they describe them differently.
reading: Each Gospel tells of women coming to Jesus' tomb early on the first day of the week. In Matthew 28:2 to 7, an angel of the Lord rolls back the stone and sits on it. His face is like lightning and his clothing white as snow. In Mark 16:5 the women see a young man in a long white robe sitting inside. In Luke 24:4 two men stand by them in shining clothes. In John 20:12, Mary Magdalene sees two angels in white, one at the head and one at the feet of where the body had lain.

Readers have handled these differences in two main ways. Some *harmonize* the accounts, fitting them together into one fuller story. On that view, one writer may simply mention the angel who spoke. Others see each Gospel as passing on its own form of the story, told for its own readers. Both kinds of readers note that the core message is the same in every account. He is not here. He is risen.

The descriptions also show something found across the Bible. Messenger angels often look like men. In Genesis 18, three visitors come to Abraham as travelers. In Mark and Luke, the tomb messengers are called a young man and men, and Luke later calls them angels (24:23). Many readers note that shining clothes and sudden appearing, not wings, are what usually mark these messengers in the text.

words.d: to fit different accounts of one event together into a single story
the Gospels' account of women finding Jesus' burial place open and his body gone
one telling of an event, such as each Gospel's report of the tomb

look.title: Messengers at the Tomb
look.prompt: Two Gospels describe one messenger and two describe two. How might a reader who harmonizes explain this? How might a reader who sees separate forms of the story explain it?

check.q: Which Gospel says an angel rolled back the stone and sat on it?
check.why: Matthew 28:2 says an angel of the Lord rolled back the stone and sat on it.

check.q: What does it mean to harmonize the Gospel accounts?
choices: To fit them together into one fuller story
To choose one and reject the others
check.why: Harmonizing means combining the accounts into a single story, explaining differences as different focus.

check.q: According to the reading, what usually marks messenger angels in the text?
check.why: Messenger angels often look like men, marked by shining clothes and sudden appearing, not by wings.

lessons.title: Raphael in Tobit
lessons.mainIdea: In the book of Tobit, the angel Raphael travels in disguise to help a family and then points them to God.
reading: The book of *Tobit* is a Jewish story probably written around 200 BCE. Copies in Aramaic and Hebrew were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls. It is in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles. Protestants place it among the *Apocrypha*, books read for learning but not counted as Scripture. It tells of Tobit, a faithful man living in exile in Nineveh, and his son Tobias.

Tobias must make a long journey to collect money his father left in Media. A guide offers to go with him, calling himself Azarias. The two travel together. Along the way the guide helps Tobias catch a fish, arrange his marriage to a young woman named Sarah, and return home safely. At the end, Tobit's eyesight is restored. Only then does the guide reveal who he is.

In Tobit 12, he says he is *Raphael*, one of the seven holy angels who stand before God. His name means "God heals." He tells the family to thank God, not him, and says he came by God's will. He adds that they never truly saw him eat. Tobit shows how Second Temple Jewish writers could picture angels as named, caring messengers who still point beyond themselves to God.

words.d: a Jewish story of about 200 BCE, in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, in which Raphael guides a family
books found in some Bibles that Protestants read for learning but do not count as Scripture
the angel in Tobit whose name means God heals

look.title: Raphael Reveals Himself
look.text: Raphael tells Tobit and Tobias that he is one of the seven holy angels who present the prayers of the holy ones and go in before the glory of the Holy One. He tells them not to be afraid, and to bless God and give thanks to him forever.
look.cite: Tobit 12:15-18, paraphrased from the Greek text
look.prompt: How does Raphael's answer here compare with the angel's answer to John in Revelation 22?

check.q: What name does the angel use while traveling with Tobias?
check.why: In Tobit 5 the guide calls himself Azarias. He reveals he is Raphael only in chapter 12.

check.q: How do Protestant Bibles usually treat the book of Tobit?
choices: As part of the Hebrew Bible
As a book of the Talmud
check.why: Protestants place Tobit in the Apocrypha. Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include it as Scripture.

check.q: What does Raphael tell the family to do once he reveals himself?
choices: Bless God and give thanks to him
check.why: In Tobit 12 Raphael points the family away from himself and tells them to thank God.

lessons.title: Testing Popular Ideas
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser urged readers to test popular ideas about angels against what the texts actually say.
reading: Many ideas about angels come from movies, greeting cards and later traditions. In Angels (2018), Heiser urged readers to go back to the texts and check. Some popular ideas turn out to fit the Bible well. Others add details the Bible never gives. A careful reader can sort them by asking, "Which verse says this?"

Here are three examples. First, many people picture every angel with wings. In the texts, the winged beings are mostly cherubim and seraphim. Messengers like the visitors in Genesis 18 or the angel in Judges 13 appear as men. Daniel 9:21 is sometimes read as Gabriel flying, but the Hebrew there is unclear. Second, many people say the dead become angels. Heiser showed that the Bible keeps angels and humans distinct. Third, many think the Bible names many angels. The Protestant Bible names only two.

Heiser also spent years answering the *ancient astronaut* theory. This is the claim that beings from other planets visited early humans and were remembered as gods or angels. Some writers say Ezekiel's vision in Ezekiel 1 describes a spacecraft. Heiser argued that such claims misread the ancient languages. Ezekiel 1:28 itself calls what the prophet saw the likeness of the glory of the LORD. Checking the *context* of a verse is often the quickest test.

words.d: the claim, rejected by Heiser, that visitors from other planets were remembered as gods or angels
the words, verses and setting around a passage that shape its meaning
the ideas and images spread by movies, songs, cards and other everyday media

look.title: Check the Claim
look.text: Claim A: every angel has wings. Claim B: a grandparent who dies becomes an angel. Claim C: Ezekiel 1 describes a spacecraft. Tools: Genesis 18:2, Judges 13:6, Hebrews 12:22-23, Ezekiel 1:28.
look.prompt: Choose one claim. Use one of the listed verses to test it, and explain in two or three sentences what the verse shows.

check.q: According to the reading, which beings are mostly the winged ones in the texts?
check.why: Wings are described mostly for cherubim and seraphim. Messenger angels often appear as men.

check.q: What does Ezekiel 1:28 call what the prophet saw?
choices: The likeness of the glory of the LORD
check.why: Ezekiel 1:28 names the vision as the likeness of the glory of the LORD, which is the text's own explanation.

check.q: What is the ancient astronaut theory?
choices: The claim that visitors from other planets were remembered as gods or angels
check.why: The ancient astronaut theory says off-world visitors became the gods of old stories. Heiser argued against it from the ancient languages.

lessons.title: Angels in Art and Music
lessons.mainIdea: Artists and composers have retold the Bible's angel scenes for centuries, adding details of their own.
reading: Around 1320, the poet Dante finished his Paradiso, the last part of his Divine Comedy. In it he pictures the nine orders of angels circling God in rings of light, following Pseudo-Dionysius. In 1512 the painter Raphael finished the Sistine Madonna. Two small winged children lean on a ledge at the bottom of the painting. These *putti* became some of the most copied angels in the world.

Music carried the angel scenes too. Charles Wesley's Christmas hymn, now known as Hark! The Herald Angels Sing, was first published in 1739. George Frideric Handel composed Messiah in 1741. One of its choruses sets the angels' words from Luke 2:14, "Glory to God in the highest." Choirs in Chicago and around the world still perform Messiah each winter.

Art and music are forms of *interpretation*. Each artist chooses what to show and adds details the text does not give, such as halos, harps, feathered wings or baby faces. A reader can enjoy such works and still know where their details come from. A good habit is to ask of any image: which verse is this showing, and what has the artist added?

words.d: winged baby figures in Renaissance art, often mistaken for biblical cherubim
a way of explaining or showing what a text means
Handel's 1741 musical work setting Bible passages, including the angels' song in Luke 2

look.title: Angels in Art and Music Through Time
look.cite: Standard dates for Dante's Divine Comedy, Raphael's Sistine Madonna, Charles Wesley's hymn and Handel's Messiah
look.prompt: Which of these works follows a Bible text closely, and which adds the most detail of its own? Explain one choice.

check.q: Which work pictures the nine orders of angels circling God?
check.why: Dante's Paradiso pictures the nine orders in rings of light, following Pseudo-Dionysius.

check.q: Which Bible verse does a famous chorus in Handel's Messiah set?
check.why: The chorus sets the angels' words from Luke 2:14, "Glory to God in the highest."

check.q: According to the reading, what is a good question to ask of any angel image?
choices: Which verse is this showing, and what has the artist added?
Is the artist Catholic or Protestant?
How many wings does it have?
check.why: The reading suggests asking which verse an image shows and what the artist added beyond the text.

review.q: What does the angel tell John in Revelation 19:10 and 22:9?
review.why: Both times the angel refuses worship, calls himself a fellow servant and says, "worship God."

review.q: Which three New Testament passages say the law came through angels?
review.why: Stephen in Acts 7:53, Paul in Galatians 3:19 and Hebrews 2:2 all speak of angels at the giving of the law.

review.q: Which ancient version names angels at God's right hand in Deuteronomy 33:2?
choices: The Songs of the Sabbath Sacrifice
review.why: The Greek Septuagint reads angels with God at his right hand; the Hebrew speaks of holy ones.

review.q: How do the two main readings of Colossians 2:18 differ?
choices: One says Paul wrote it, one says Peter did
One reads Hebrew, one reads Latin
One is about Sinai, one is about the tomb
One means worship given to angels; the other means joining the angels' own worship
review.why: The Greek phrase can mean worship directed to angels or the worship angels offer, which some teachers claimed to join.

review.q: In which book does an angel guide a young man named Tobias on a journey?
review.why: In Tobit, Raphael, calling himself Azarias, guides Tobias to Media and home again.

review.q: What do all four Gospel accounts of the empty tomb share?
choices: An angel sitting on the stone
The message that Jesus is not there but risen
A vision of the heavenly host singing
review.why: The accounts differ in details, but each gives the core message that Jesus is not in the tomb and is risen.

review.q: What do the Songs of the Sabbath Sacrifice picture?
choices: Angels serving as priests in a heavenly sanctuary
Angels giving the law to Moses
Angels guarding the tree of life
review.why: The Songs, found at Qumran and Masada, describe heavenly beings praising God as priests in a heavenly temple.

review.q: Which popular idea about angels comes mostly from Renaissance art?
review.why: Renaissance putti, like those in Raphael's Sistine Madonna, turned cherubs into winged babies. The texts describe guardians.
